The equilibrium temperature of a planet on a circular orbit around a given star depends on the stellar flux it receives:

\[
T_{\rm eq}\propto \left(\frac{L_*(1-A)}{a^2}\right)^{1/4}
\]

where \(L_*\) is the star’s luminosity, \(A\) is the bond albedo and \(a\) is the semi‑major axis.  
Since all three planets orbit the same star and have the same albedo (\(A=0.3\)), the luminosity and albedo cancel when we take ratios. Thus

\[
T_{\rm eq}\propto a^{-1/2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad a\propto T_{\rm eq}^{-2}.
\]

Kepler’s third law for planets much lighter than the star gives

\[
P^2\propto a^3\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad P\propto a^{3/2}.
\]

Combining the two relations:

\[
P\propto \bigl(T_{\rm eq}^{-2}\bigr)^{3/2}=T_{\rm eq}^{-3}.
\]

Hence the orbital period scales as the inverse cube of the equilibrium temperature.

---

### Temperature ratios

Given  
\(T_1/T_2 \approx 1.4\) and \(T_2/T_3 \approx 2.3\),

\[
\frac{T_1}{T_3}= \frac{T_1}{T_2}\times\frac{T_2}{T_3}=1.4\times2.3\approx3.22.
\]

So

\[
\frac{P_3}{P_1}= \left(\frac{T_1}{T_3}\right)^{3}\approx (3.22)^{3}\approx 33.4.
\]

---

The mass ratios supplied (1.15 and 1.35) are not needed for the period ratio because the planetary masses are negligible compared with the host star.

\[
\boxed{\text{P_3 is about }33\text{ times larger than P_1.}}
\]

Answer: D
